channel.description: Keeping DFIR Intelligence on your Radar. The latest DFIR research from hundreds of sources, ranked by relevance for practitioners.

item.title: Hackers backdoor Linux servers using trojanized CWP web server
item.description:
CWPdoor, a passive Linux backdoor, is trojanizing the cwpsrv binary on Control Web Panel servers, suppressing its own access log entries and sitting silent until a cryptographically authenticated HTTP header triggers execution.
Key findings:
- The infection chain begins with a script disguised as a CWP updater. It replaces legitimate cwpsrv binaries at versions 1.15.10 and 1.24.0 with the malicious CWPdoor build, then covers its tracks by restoring original file and directory timestamps, deleting temp files, and wiping command history. The swap is designed to look like nothing changed.
- CWPdoor is a passive backdoor: it stays completely dormant until an attacker sends a specially crafted HTTP request carrying three custom headers: X-Ngx-Integrity-Data (the encrypted command), X-Ngx-Integrity-Time (a timestamp), and X-Ngx-Integrity-Sig (an RSA signature). The backdoor validates that the timestamp is within a plus-or-minus 300-second window and verifies the RSA signature before it will decrypt and execute anything. All command traffic uses AES-256-CBC. This replay-protection design means passive scanning of the wire alone will not expose it.
- The malware actively patches the server's logging module so the triggering HTTP request never appears in access logs. Standard web server log review will produce a clean record even on a fully compromised host, making log-based detection unreliable as a sole source of truth.
- XLab spotted the initial infection script on June 29. On September 30, a VirusTotal upload surfaced an archive pairing CWPdoor with the Ebury Linux backdoor and credential-stealing botnet, which ESET documented in May 2024 as having compromised nearly 400,000 servers since 2009. The malicious cwpsrv file in that archive, named cwpsrv.suspeito, had zero detections at time of upload. The relationship between Ebury and CWPdoor is unconfirmed, but co-packaging suggests at minimum shared infrastructure or operators.
- Exposure is significant: XLab observed more than 340,000 CWP instances reachable from the public internet over the past month. Any host running an unverified cwpsrv binary is a candidate for compromise.
Practitioner takeaway: On any CWP host, check for the ngx_http_integrity_helper Unix socket, inspect running processes for suspicious cwpsrv helper children, and grep the cwpsrv binary itself for the string X-Ngx-Integrity. Because the backdoor suppresses its own access log entries, log review is insufficient: compare the on-disk cwpsrv binary hash against a known-good copy from the official package. If compromise is confirmed, replace the binary, upgrade CWP to the latest release, rotate all control panel credentials, and treat the host as fully compromised pending a broader investigation for secondary implants including Ebury.

item.title: Hacking on Autopilot: Inside ARTEX Cybercrime Campaigns
item.description:
Agentic hacking platform ARTEX, backed by Chinese 🇨🇳 LLMs running almost entirely without human input, has driven opportunistic cybercrime campaigns across certificate theft, crypto draining, and gaming account harvesting at industrial scale.
Key findings:
- Check Point Research identified 2,557 systems hosting or having hosted ARTEX panels, with 1,608 live and publicly accessible at research time. Ten misconfigured instances exposed full databases, revealing operator prompts, model selections, and complete agent action logs. The largest share of live C2 servers is hosted in the US 🇺🇸 (882, 54%), followed by Hong Kong (295, 18%) and China 🇨🇳 (103, 6%). Three infrastructure clusters were identified by shared version tags, ASN, and co-hosted services, pointing to coordinated operator groups running fleets of hundreds of hosts.
- Chinese 🇨🇳 AI models dominated configured LLMs across the ten exposed instances, with the Deepseek Flash family most prevalent. The only guardrail hits observed came from Anthropic's Opus 5.5, after which operators switched to permissive Chinese 🇨🇳 models. One two-week Apple certificate campaign processed 36 billion tokens across two parallel ARTEX consoles at an estimated cost of $700-$1,500. Operators barely typed: the most common prompts translated to "what's the progress?" and "which task is closest to the goal?"
- Attack techniques across campaigns included hardcoded admin credentials in SPA JavaScript bundles, missing authentication on web APIs, RCE via command injection and Server Side Template Injection (SSTI), Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR), and Linux privilege escalation through overly permissive folder access. One campaign chain reached supply chain compromise: an unauthenticated API leaked AWS S3 credentials granting write access to a bucket serving 714 iOS enterprise-signed IPA landing pages, and the agent autonomously reasoned through, executed, and verified manifest poisoning before the bucket owner restored the original file.
- Campaign outcomes: 300-plus Apple .p12 code-signing certificates and plaintext passwords stolen, with three passing full validation (OCSP, key-cert match, expiry, matching In-House provisioning profile). A crypto-draining operation across 292 targets found multiple RCEs and database dumps but transferred $0, partly because agent "success" verdicts were hallucinations based on API responses. A gaming account campaign recovered over 190,000 Honor of Kings credential sets from a plaintext static file in a web root, with roughly 6,000 accounts confirmed still valid by agent-driven stratified sampling.
- ARTEX exposes a version tag in its panel that functions as a clustering artifact. Unique tags combined with shared ASN and co-hosted services allowed high-confidence grouping of three distinct operator clusters. The project went closed-source on October 8 after attacks on South Korean 🇰🇷 banks, but maintained forks keep it available. Related frameworks observed in the wild include CyberStrike, Cairn, PentAGI, and custom-built platforms like "PZZ."
Defender takeaway: exposed ARTEX panels are themselves a detection surface. Scan your external IP ranges and threat-intel feeds for the ARTEX web dashboard fingerprint and version tags. Internally, the attack chain leaves artifacts that standard perimeter logging should catch: unauthenticated API calls to credential or wallet endpoints, repeated IDOR probing across sequential object IDs, child processes spawned from web service accounts consistent with SSTI or command injection, and S3 write events from unexpected principals against buckets serving static app content. The report's IOC table covers identified C2 IPs and infrastructure; pull those for blocklist and retrospective log review. Any organization running iOS enterprise distribution, crypto payment infrastructure, or gray-market adjacent services should treat agentic scanning as a baseline threat, not a future one.

item.title: Attackers Actively Probing for Upgrade-Window RCE Vulnerability in WordPress Core
item.description:
CVE-2026-119977 (CVSS 8.1) is an unauthenticated RCE in WordPress core 4.7 through 7.1.3, exploitable during the brief upgrade window. Active exploitation began on disclosure day, October 28, 2026, and is now in CISA's KEV catalog.
Key findings:
- The root cause is predictable, web-accessible staging paths created during full-package core upgrades. WordPress extracts update files to /wp-content/upgrade/wordpress-[version]/ before completing the swap, and the installer PHP files there are reachable from the web during that window. An unauthenticated attacker who hits setup-config.php during that window can complete the staged installation, create a rogue administrator account, and upload arbitrary PHP. The attack pattern observed in the report is a GET request to paths like /wp-content/upgrade/wordpress-6.9.11/setup-config.php.
- Exploitation is a race condition, difficult but not theoretical. Over 240,000 exploit attempts have been blocked since disclosure, peaking at over 74,000 on October 30, 2026. The volume reflects mass automated scanning to the predictable path, not precision timing, meaning attackers are sending bulk requests and betting on hitting sites mid-upgrade.
- Top attacking IPs from the report: 103.59.160[.]171 (over 74,900 blocked requests), 2001:df1:e8c0::106b (over 40,400), 51.89.103[.]78 (over 34,600), 185.177.72[.]61, 195.3.220[.]7, 96.62.218[.]148, 20.217.186[.]29, 87.58.197[.]83, 154.26.238[.]8, and 20.46.43[.]126.
- Patched versions span every supported branch from 4.7.39 through 7.1.4. Because the vulnerable upgrade routine runs one final time when applying the patch from an affected version, the update itself briefly exposes the window. The mitigation before patching is to block external HTTP access to PHP files under /wp-content/upgrade/ at the web server level, removing the attacker's ability to reach the installer even if the timing is right.
- Post-compromise artifacts to review: unexpected files or directories remaining under /wp-content/upgrade/, newly created administrator accounts, unfamiliar plugins, and web shells or backdoor PHP dropped to the document root or plugin directories. The report notes absence of access log entries does not rule out compromise.
Hunt your web server access logs for any GET or POST requests targeting PHP files under /wp-content/upgrade/, especially setup-config.php. Flag requests from the IPs above as high priority. Then audit WordPress user tables and the installed plugin list for accounts or additions created around October 28 through November 1, 2026. Patch to 7.1.4 or the branch equivalent, and block /wp-content/upgrade/*.php at the web server before you trigger the update if you have not done so already.

item.description:
Attackers are abusing stolen Entra ID application client secrets to authenticate as legitimate workloads, bypassing user-centric identity controls entirely and potentially accessing Graph, Key Vault, SharePoint, and Azure DevOps.
Key details:
- The attack vector is non-human identity: threat actors using stolen client secrets authenticate as service principals, not users, meaning no password spray, no MFA to bypass, and no user sign-in to alert on. Depending on permissions granted to the compromised app, often years ago and never reviewed, the attacker lands with the same access as the application itself.
- Two Entra ID error codes surface attacker reconnaissance and credential stuffing against application secrets: AADSTS7000215 (invalid client secret) and AADSTS7000222 (expired client secret). These codes appear in both EntraIdSignInEvents and EntraIdSpnSignInEvents in Microsoft Defender XDR, and the hunt query published in the report unions both tables to cover the full identity surface.
- The KQL hunt filters both tables for those two error codes over the last seven days, tags each result with its source table (UserSignIns or ServicePrincipalSignIns), and enriches with Application, IPAddress, Country, and an ErrorDescription field derived via a case statement. The full query is in the report.
- Risk triage is not binary: a single failure from an internal deployment pipeline is noise. The signal is clusters of failures from unusual source IPs, failures followed by successful authentications from the same IP or application, and applications with broad permissions that have never been audited. The report explicitly deprioritizes static IP-based IOCs because they rotate; the focus is indicators of attack behavior.
- Service principals are a persistent blind spot in identity monitoring. Most detection engineering effort targets regular Entra ID users. If your org uses service principals, they are part of the identity attack surface and need coverage in authentication hunting, even if the detection logic differs from user-focused rules.
Practitioner takeaway: Run the union query from the report against EntraIdSignInEvents and EntraIdSpnSignIns, then pivot on any IP with repeated failures that also has a successful authentication event in the same window. From there, pull the application's current API permissions in Entra ID and check audit logs for resource access after the successful auth. That sequence, failure cluster, then success, then permission scope, then downstream access, is the investigation chain that separates a stale config from an active intrusion.

item.title: Supply chain attack: BO Team in a software developer's infrastructure
item.description:
BO Team APT nearly pulled off a software supply chain attack against a Russian 🇷🇺 software developer, fully compromising CI/CD infrastructure, a code-signing server, and every major IT component over several months before detection.
Key findings:
- Initial access came through SSH exposed to the internet on a Linux terminal server using a service account with password auth enabled. From there, BO Team exploited CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell) against an unpatched VMware vCenter 7.0.3 instance, obtaining a root shell via a netcat reverse shell (nc -e /bin/sh) and reading /root/.ssh/id_rsa directly off the hypervisor. This single pivot gave them footing across two virtualization clusters and cascaded into the GitLab server, Ansible orchestration system, backup servers, the corporate VPN, and ultimately the SIEM itself. The attackers read a plaintext password from an LDAP comment field to compromise the proxy account, found domain credentials stored in world-readable service scripts, and brute-forced the root SSH account of a Linux admin's personal terminal server (~2500 attempts, PermitRootLogin yes enabled). The krbtgt key was extracted via ntdsutil.exe copying ntds.dit plus registry export for decryption, enabling a Golden Ticket path to every domain in the forest.
- Persistence on Linux hypervisors and VMs was established through cron.hourly entries disguised as system components: /etc/cron.hourly/pgcache (MD5: 346b04985ec6c5d107ba0ddf32fe7691, HEUR:Backdoor[.]Shell.Agent.o) masquerading as a PostgreSQL component, and /etc/cron.hourly/1vmware-timesync launching the obfuscated loader /usr/bin/vmware-toolbox-setdate (MD5: 5aa8c19c897176502cf8d8fc543fafc7, Trojan[.]Shell.Agent.gc). That loader decrypts an AES-256-CBC payload in memory into /proc/self/fd/3 and executes a ReverseSSH backdoor (MD5: 68957de915e2a58339fa477f8078bdf4, HEUR:HackTool.Linux.ReverseSSH.gen) connecting outbound to vmware-timecheck-api.nofrillsdns[.]com:443. All backdoor files had timestomping applied. C2 domains were created on the free nofrillsdns[.]com service and default to 127.0.0.1 when inactive, activating only on DNS record change.
- On Windows, lsass dumping via Nanodump was blocked, so BO Team fell back to a fully LoLBIN technique: rundll32.exe calling comsvcs.dll ordinal 24 (MiniDumpW) through a cmd.exe /Q chain, writing the dump to Windows\Temp\pnSsW4wSk.cur, then exfiltrating it over SSH via the built-in C:\Windows\System32\OpenSSH\scp.exe to their terminal server foothold. On the code-signing server specifically, blocked detections of PDM:Exploit.Win32.Generic on WmiPrvSE.exe and PDM:Trojan.Win32.GenAutorunSchedulerTaskRun.b on svchost.exe indicate attempted WMI-based backdoor installation and scheduled task creation that the security solution caught, but only because it happened to be present there.
- After network isolation, BO Team sent phishing emails with a valid DKIM signature using the stolen private key from the compromised mail server, routed through ip-223-6.dataclub[.]info. The SPF check passed. This is a critical post-incident artifact: a DKIM-signed phishing email from an attacker is evidence of prior mail server compromise, not a new intrusion vector. The attacker VPN source IPs were 193.3.23[.]236 and 80.76.42[.]139 (Lviv, Ukraine 🇺🇦 provider). C2 IP 95.81.115[.]77 appeared after defenders isolated the network and BO Team tried to reactivate backdoors, delivering a Global Socket utility with hardcoded key maiShei3ohchoh9UtekairoPhaiz5ja8 via gsocket[.]io.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt /etc/cron.hourly/ for entries masquerading as database or VMware components, check file modify timestamps against creation timestamps for timestomping, and grep /dev/shm/ for credential harvesting files left by modified NX login binaries. On Windows, look for rundll32.exe invoking comsvcs.dll with lsass PID arguments and scp.exe making outbound connections, which are reliable BO Team lsass-dump-and-exfil signatures. If you are responding post-isolation and receive DKIM-valid inbound email that did not originate from your mail server infrastructure, treat it as confirmation the attacker held your private DKIM key: rotate it immediately and treat the mail server as fully compromised. Full IOCs including 9 file hashes and 7 domains/IPs are in the Kaspersky ICS CERT report.

If you are responding post-isolation and receive DKIM-valid inbound email that did not originate from your mail server infrastructure, treat it as confirmation the attacker held your private DKIM key: rotate it immediately and treat the mail server as fully compromised. Full IOCs including 9 file hashes and 7 domains/IPs are in the Kaspersky ICS CERT report.

item.title: VAPOR PANDA hackers use multi-agent AI to target government, pharmaceutical, semiconductor, defense organizations
item.description:
Chinese 🇨🇳 APT VAPOR PANDA ran a 11-day AI-coordinated espionage blitz against 200+ orgs across 14 countries, using the ARTEX agentic framework and DeepSeek to run parallel intrusions at a scale no manual operation could match.
Key details:
- Starting Oct. 17, 2026, VAPOR PANDA targeted foreign ministries across Latin America, Europe, Asia, and the Middle East, plus US 🇺🇸 semiconductor, defense, think tank, and pharmaceutical organizations. CrowdStrike OverWatch confirmed post-exploitation at nine organizations, where the attackers deployed the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor, conducted credential spraying, network scanning, and reconnaissance. BLOODALCHEMY was disguised inside a legitimate loader, staged in exposed open directories, and communicated back to VAPOR PANDA infrastructure.
- ARTEX coordinates a main agent with subordinate planner and worker agents through a shared graph of facts, findings, and goals. Recovered operator transcripts were written in Chinese 🇨🇳, marked as human instruction, and timestamped in China 🇨🇳 Standard Time. The operator directed agents to create web shells, extract domain administrator passwords, and explicitly identify Windows machines lacking endpoint sensor coverage, using Chinese 🇨🇳 red-team slang for the EDR product.
- The attack chains were sophisticated and varied by target. At one US 🇺🇸 pharmaceutical organization, the agent chained an unsigned SAML assertion with an XXE flaw to query the cloud Instance Metadata Service, escalating to an enterprise administrator account. At a second, it deployed web shells, abused an unauthenticated orchestration service for root access in production containers, read LAPS passwords, and abused resource-based constrained delegation. Against a Greek 🇬🇷 government entity, the agent used authentication keys from a 2022 mail server directory export that had never been rotated, forged an administrator token, read mailboxes, and pivoted to the internal network using VPN credentials recovered from a user's sent mail.
- A single intrusion consumed approximately 1.4 billion input tokens, illustrating the automated scale. ARTEX is built on open-source components layered over commercial LLM subscriptions including DeepSeek, making this toolchain reproducible from largely public resources. CrowdStrike assesses this VAPOR PANDA campaign is distinct from industry reporting under the Storm-0940 designation, suggesting ARTEX is gaining traction across multiple China-nexus groups.
- This marks VAPOR PANDA's first observed use of AI-driven intrusion tooling and a significant expansion from its 2021-era targeting of government, think tank, energy, and extractive sectors into pharmaceuticals, semiconductors, nuclear, and defense, across new geographic regions.
Takeaway for responders: Rotate all signing keys, preauthentication keys, and service credentials after any suspected data exposure, including material in historical backups and directory exports. Enforce SAML signature validation and require IMDSv2. Hunt for ARTEX markers in command-line parameters as CrowdStrike's report directs. Prioritize patching internet-facing appliances, particularly long-lived Linux-based servers. The sensor-coverage enumeration step means unmanaged hosts are actively being selected for follow-on compromise: audit your EDR deployment gaps before the adversary maps them for you.

item.title: New Lindnor Backdoor and Glut of Security Killers Used in Ransomware Attack on U.S. Org
item.description:
Anubis-focused ransomware crew deploys previously undocumented Lindnor backdoor and 13 security-killer tools in a single hour, targeting a U.S. 🇺🇸 org running Microsoft SQL Server in October 2026.
Key details:
- Backdoor.Lindnor, the custom implant at the center of this attack, masqueraded as a Chrome component unpacker (healthcontroller64.exe) on one SQL Server and as a VMware helper (svchelper.exe) on another, running as a service in both cases. It beaconed system metadata including process ID, OS version, file path, computer name, username, domain, and logon server to a primary C2 and a fallback, both over port 443. C2s: msrcontrib[.]com and cfgsync-relay.eastus.cloudapp[.]azure[.]com. Three Lindnor hashes are in the report (fc200686175559f4544a5de826905f09a68476d889690a3be40ac32356790cb8, 5d2dd9caf2ae4a5083dbec16e688040456cdbc31eaeecbab78188e322ed0415b, ad9575a9ef2dcc9d2fd2a24376c418549d4b3db5564c22b20081d33cf7629e43). The same backdoor appeared on two other unrelated organizations without ransomware follow-through, suggesting it may serve as a persistent staging implant across separate operations.
- Within roughly an hour the attackers dropped at least 13 executables targeting security products, 11 of them previously unpublished, plus 5 publicly known vulnerable drivers (havoc.sys, monprocessex.sys, xhunter1.sys, bdapiutil64.sys, fly.sys) for BYOVD kernel-level access. Two tools, gbbsym.exe and symgooq.exe, impersonated Symantec software and accepted a -l switch to list kernel callbacks and a -d switch to remove them. Only huntreagent.exe and s1.exe ran unblocked; both share the same file size but carry different hashes, suggesting two builds of one tool.
- The attackers registered AnyDesk as a Safe Mode with Networking service using: reg.exe add HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SafeBoot\Network\AnyDesk /ve /t REG_SZ /d Service /f. The dedicated tool safemode.exe (hash 47a864736764112d7897c76e56d51111ce75b3e46fdbac6933df8a5b29507d17) automated this. A new local account was created and added to a local group alongside this. Because security software does not fully operate in Safe Mode, this gives the BYOVD drivers a clean window to strip kernel callbacks and disable protections before full encryption.
- The Anubis payload (iservice.exe, e69b882218fa2a19fd351741874bfcd10a6ae91076e6a8483795e0e357f8d026) was blocked before execution. Had it run, it appends .anubis to encrypted files and drops ransom notes named restore files.txt and restore files.html. It also carries an optional wiper mode that empties file contents entirely rather than encrypting them. Hawkmoth, the RaaS operator behind Anubis, rebranded from Sphinx ransomware in December 2024 with the payload largely unchanged. The group has claimed roughly 96 victims in the past 12 months, 52% of them in the U.S..
Practitioner takeaway: Initial access was not identified, but both affected machines were Microsoft SQL Servers, making them a natural pivot point for initial triage. Hunt for services named or hosting healthcontroller64.exe or svchelper.exe in Chrome or VMware directory paths, and check for the HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SafeBoot\Network\AnyDesk registry key as a high-confidence indicator of Safe Mode persistence staging. Any of the five named vulnerable drivers loaded from non-standard paths alongside a new local account creation should be treated as a confirmed pre-ransomware pattern. Full IOCs and file hashes are in the Symantec report.

item.title: CWPdoor: The Invisible Backdoor Living Inside Control Web Panel
item.description:
CWPdoor is a passive, log-suppressing backdoor compiled directly into the Control Web Panel web server binary, with zero detections on VirusTotal and confirmed victims already in the wild across more than 340,000 internet-exposed CWP instances.
Key findings:
- The infection chain begins with cwpsrv_update.sh (MD5: e505d4ffa21cf494a5dc2d7c8f4f1236), a root-level script that masquerades as a routine version update. It downloads a trojaned cwpsrv binary from 136.0.141[.]71, backs up the original, overwrites /usr/local/cwpsrv/bin/cwpsrv, then deliberately restores the file's atime/mtime and the parent directory timestamp to their pre-infection values and purges command history with "history -d". Under a standard ls or stat check, the replaced binary looks untouched, which makes filesystem timeline forensics unreliable here without deeper integrity verification.
- The backdoor itself is not a separate process dropped alongside cwpsrv. The attacker recompiled cwpsrv with two injected functions, ngx_http_integrity_init and ngx_http_integrity_check, woven into Nginx's own request-handling pipeline. During normal operation it is indistinguishable from a legitimate server. The trigger is a specially crafted HTTP request carrying three custom headers: X-Ngx-Integrity-Time (timestamp), X-Ngx-Integrity-Data (AES-256-CBC encrypted command, Base64), and X-Ngx-Integrity-Sig (RSA signature). The embedded RSA public key is XOR-obfuscated with 0x55. The ±300-second timestamp window and RSA signature binding provide replay protection, meaning only the operator holding the private key can issue commands.
- Once verified, the master process decrypts the command and passes it to a helper child process over a Unix domain socket named ngx_http_integrity_helper for execution. Results are AES-encrypted and returned in an HTTP 200 response typed as application/octet-stream. Critically, the backdoor tampers with the per-request module context array to null out the logging module pointer, so the trigger request never appears in access logs. The forensic trail is actively erased at the application layer.
- A file named evidencia.tgz was uploaded to VirusTotal from Brazil 🇧🇷 on September 30, 2026, containing both the Ebury SSH backdoor (libkeyutils[.]so.1.5.2) and cwpsrv.suspeito, the cwpdoor binary, with zero vendor detections on the latter. This confirms real-world victims exist. Two cwpdoor samples are documented: MD5 965aea67fb40de1bab5169ada993349f (cwpsrv 1.15.10) and MD5 d3f4e95113d49ab3991b45e457bda75b (cwpsrv 1.24.0). The downloader infrastructure resolves to 136.0.141[.]71, with payloads served from hxxp://136.0.141[.]71/static/cwpsrv_1.15.10 and hxxp://136.0.141[.]71/static/cwpsrv_1.24.0.
- Three fast triage commands from the report: run "ss -axp | grep integrity" to check for the ngx_http_integrity_helper Unix socket, run "ps aux | grep cwpsrv" to look for anomalous helper child processes, and run "strings /usr/local/cwpsrv/bin/cwpsrv | grep X-Ngx-Integrity" to detect injected header strings in the binary. If infected, the attacker's own backup of the original binary sits at /usr/local/cwpsrv/bin/cwpsrv.prev-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S) and can be used for restoration. Rotate all CWP credentials immediately and treat the host as fully compromised given arbitrary command execution capability.
Practitioner takeaway: Do not rely on filesystem timestamps or access logs to rule out this compromise. The infection script explicitly restores both. The socket check ("ss -axp | grep integrity") and the strings grep against the live binary are your fastest on-host pivots. IOCs and sample hashes are in the XLab report.

item.title: The SOC Files 5: Ghost in the pipeline, or a fileless SharePoint breach by Storm-2603
item.description:
Storm-2603 exploited ToolShell (CVE-2025-53770/53771) in on-premises SharePoint to deploy a fully fileless webshell inside w3wp.exe, later pivoting to Warlock ransomware after weeks of stealthy access.
Key findings:
- The intrusion followed a deliberate timing strategy. A fingerprinting probe on Dec 20 (consistent with ONYPHE's active vulnerability checker) was followed by three days of silence, then full RCE execution on Christmas Eve (Dec 24) when security staffing is typically reduced. The gap caused the initial probe to be triaged as low priority and delayed correlation until retrospective analysis. Attribution to Storm-2603 rests on the ToolShell exploitation pattern, Warlock-linked EDR killer (C:\programdata\rsndispot.sys, MD5 054a32d6033b1744dca7f49b2e466ea2), and Velociraptor abuse previously documented by Cisco Talos in October 2025.
- The webshell (vskp2, MD5 0xFD91321BF7FF7245DDA9B7B5D791ACE8) never touched disk. It was injected directly into the ASP.NET runtime inside w3wp.exe, persisting for the lifetime of the application domain. The main orchestrator G.cs registered a custom VirtualPathProvider via reflection to hook ASP.NET's virtual-path processing, used GetCacheKey() as the interception point, and filtered traffic by a specific User-Agent header so the implant stayed dormant against unrecognized requests. C2 used a custom binary protocol with XOR obfuscation over HTTP, blending into normal SharePoint traffic. The suo5 tool implemented full-duplex TCP tunneling to pivot inside the target network, all proxied through the SharePoint host.
- Post-exploitation moved aggressively once the in-memory bridge was established. w3wp.exe spawned msiexec.exe to silently install a Velociraptor MSI (version 0.73.4.0, vulnerable to CVE-2025-6264) fetched from hxxps://vdfccjpnedujhrzscjtq.supabase[.]co/storage/v1/object/public/image/v4[.]msi. Storm-2603 then deployed layered persistence: Zoho Assist Unattended (fetched from hxxps://files.catbox[.]moe/8f7vex[.]msi), VS Code CLI tunneling (MD5 0x3D553B9061C03F891CE97D7D2E64DDEE), Cloudflare Tunnel (hxxps://github[.]com/cloudflare/cloudflared/releases/latest/download/cloudflared-windows-amd64[.]msi), and a lightweight reverse proxy. Privilege escalation used EfsPotato's named-pipe impersonation via EFSRPC to coerce LSASS.exe and obtain a SYSTEM token without dropping a standalone binary.
- For detection, the Kaspersky report points to two reliable runtime signals. For deserialization exploitation: watch CLR loader events for Microsoft.GeneratedCode appearing in the same application domain as App_Web_toolpane.aspx immediately after a request to the ToolPane endpoint. Scan process memory and helper assemblies for strings including ObjectDataProvider, ExpandedWrapper, and LosFormatter. For the VPP-based memory shell: use the Microsoft-Windows-IIS-Configuration ETW provider. Events 25 and 47 record path-to-physical mappings; events 17, 18, 19, and 21 track the FileChangeNotificationMonitor chain for disk-backed files. A virtual path showing positive events 25/47 with no corresponding events 17/18/19/21 and no matching file on disk is the primary indicator of a memory-resident implant.
Hunt priority: query ETW for w3wp.exe making outbound TCP connections to non-Microsoft infrastructure, spawning msiexec.exe, or touching samlib.dll via P/Invoke. Correlate any ToolPane endpoint requests with subsequent CLR loader events in the same application domain. The report includes full IOC tables and references CLRDeserializationExploitFinder and VirtualPathProvider Lab for detection tooling. Memory and IIS ETW telemetry must be preserved before any IIS restart, since recycling the application pool destroys the implant's runtime state permanently.

The report includes full IOC tables and references CLRDeserializationExploitFinder and VirtualPathProvider Lab for detection tooling. Memory and IIS ETW telemetry must be preserved before any IIS restart, since recycling the application pool destroys the implant's runtime state permanently.

item.title: ARTEX AI Pentest Tool: What Security Teams Need to Know
item.description:
ARTEX AI, an LLM-driven autonomous pentest framework, has been weaponized by multiple China-nexus actors against 200+ organizations across 14 countries in under four weeks of confirmed malicious use.
Key findings:
- ARTEX is a Go-written, multi-agent framework built by GitHub user Autumn-27 (China 🇨🇳) that hands an entire kill chain to cooperating LLM agents: planning, exploitation, lateral movement and exfiltration with minimal human input. It went closed source October 8, 2026, but forks including ScopeWeaver and a paid ARTEX PRO edition remain in circulation. No CVE exists. This is an offensive tool abusing existing identity and exposure weaknesses, not a patchable vulnerability.
- Vapor Panda (CrowdStrike attribution) ran the largest single campaign: one ARTEX controller, 200+ targeted organizations, 14+ countries, nine confirmed compromises over 11 days starting October 17, 2026. Post-exploitation included the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor at a Middle East-region interior ministry and a Latin American foreign ministry. The operator issued instructions in Chinese 🇨🇳. In one intrusion, planning agents consumed roughly 1.4 billion input tokens. MITRE techniques confirmed include T1190, T1078.004, T1558.003 (Kerberoasting), T1003.006 (DCSync), T1505.003 (web shells), and T1567.004: command output exfiltrated through 491 rotating webhook[.]site URLs.
- Storm-0940, a China-state-aligned actor, abused consented ConnectWise Cloud Backup application identities to attempt sign-ins across 2,250+ Microsoft 365 tenants, with failure rates peaking at 2,900 per minute. No interactive user sign-in was needed because the app identities already held consented permissions. Microsoft documented the jump from initial targeting to privileged cloud access in under three hours, and in one case just 15 minutes. ConnectWise disabled seven affected application identities on October 17, 2026.
- ARTEX leaves behavioral and artifact fingerprints a responder can hunt. On-host: the directory C:\ProgramData\artx5v\, command-line parameters containing "artx" or "artex", files matching artex-probe-*, web shells named cl1217.jsp / f1219a.jsp / z1219.jsp, and the implant path D:\ProjectX\Merman_New\. Network: machine-paced password spray waves spaced exactly one second apart, 27+ cloud enumeration events in under 30 seconds, repeated outbound requests to webhook[.]site, and C2 domains sqlserver-sqlite[.]com (89.46.234[.]50) and nginxmysql[.]com (45.153.126[.]223). Storm-0940 spray IPs include 144.172.64[.]128, 144.172.64[.]60, and 144.172.64[.]99.
- BLOODALCHEMY SHA-256 hashes tied to Vapor Panda: 49fe70419fd19b81ca8d730a6ef7c1ec71b681d60b390761070d42686c7d2068 (renamed svchost.exe), 3fb5a9fb3e2cb1d6208966bd4e55d10282d19c7250d827efa560463d60a12ee4 (graphics-hook-filter64.dll), 364251838edfcf5ef1107fa692da3c5bd9a540482449f645992830134bf807ab (graphics-hook_config.bin).
Practitioner takeaway: Audit every consented third-party application identity in Entra ID now, alert on new credentials or role assignments for service principals, and rotate any SAML signing key or mail server export key older than one year. For M365 tenants connected to ConnectWise Cloud Backup, review sign-in and audit logs from October 1, 2026 onward, searching by application ID rather than display name. Theori has published free Sigma, Suricata, YARA and ModSecurity rules built from confirmed ARTEX activity. Load them and tune for machine-paced request sequences. Preserve sign-in, audit and SIEM records before removing any application or credential: cleanup before export destroys the investigation trail.

item.title: GhostMap: The Android flaw that crashes your phone before you open the app
item.description:
GhostMap: an unpatched Android parser differential bug turns a zero-permission, zero-execution APK into a device-bricking denial-of-service, confirmed on Android 10 through Android 17 with no fix available as of publication.
Key findings:
- The root cause sits in a disagreement between two Android libraries. libziparchive bounds-checks the uncompressed size only for entries marked "stored." libandroidfw maps the uncompressed size for every entry that is not marked "deflated," treating everything else as stored without that check. An entry carrying a third method value, neither stored nor deflated, falls into the gap: libandroidfw maps it at a declared size the file never actually contains, and the kernel allows the mapping. The first read past the real end of the file produces a SIGBUS (signal 7, BUS_ADRERR). The tombstone on a Pixel 10 running Android 17 points directly at android::_FileAsset::read inside libandroidfw[.]so, with an 8 KB APK mapped across roughly 16 MB of memory and the fault address landing about 197 KB past the real file end.
- Three exploitation shapes are possible, none yet observed in the wild. First, malform the manifest and the installer crashes, leaving nothing on the device. Second, malform a resource file a system service reads post-install and system_server enters a SIGBUS crash loop every few seconds (confirmed 110 consecutive cycles, safe mode disabled, screen locked on the boot animation) with factory reset as the only reliable recovery. Third, malform the app icon and every UI path to the uninstall screen crashes while the malicious app keeps running. A fourth angle: any process calling getPackageArchiveInfo() on the crafted file also dies inside the call, a native fault that bypasses Java exception handling, which means automated scanners and analysis pipelines can be silenced the same way.
- The discovery started on Aug. 12, 2026, when a banking dropper wrapped with a packer crashed Bitdefender's emulator infrastructure during installation. The packer had incidentally broken the ZIP structure; the authors showed no awareness of the crash behavior. Bitdefender reported to Google on Aug. 20, 2026 (closed: Won't Fix / Not Reproducible) and again on Aug. 25, 2026 with a working proof of concept. Google stated the issue is outside the scope of a security update fix and forwarded it to a product team for a possible future version update. No CVE has been assigned and no patch is available. The bug class has precedent: CVE-2013-4787 (Master Key), CVE-2017-13156 (Janus), and BadPack (linked to Anatsa, Cerberus, BianLian) all exploit ZIP parser disagreements on Android; Google patched a weaker factory-reset-required DoS in CVE-2016-6724 in 2016.
- Confirmed affected surface: Android 10 through Android 17, tested on a Pixel 10 at the August 5, 2026 security patch level (build google/frankel/frankel:17/CP2A.260805.005/15828068:user/release-keys). The fault is an over-read, not memory corruption, so it does not enable code execution or privilege escalation. It is a persistent denial-of-service. Bitdefender detects the malformation as Android.Riskware.Ghostmap.rA.
Practitioner takeaway: the malformation is structural and visible before execution. Triage incoming APKs by parsing ZIP entry method fields directly: any entry carrying a method value other than 0 (stored) or 8 (deflated) that also declares an uncompressed size larger than the actual file content is a candidate. On a device already in a system_server crash loop, ADB-based deletion of the offending APK between crashes is the only non-destructive recovery path, and it only works if USB debugging was enabled before the loop began and before the first full kernel reboot. After the first reboot the crash occurs early enough in boot order that even that window closes. If you are building or auditing Android scanning pipelines, verify that APK inspection calls are wrapped to handle native faults, not just Java exceptions, or the pipeline itself becomes a target.

item.title: From Streaming to Stealing: Mirax and the Rise of Server-side Android Device Takeover in META
item.description:
Android DTO malware Mirax, sold on Russian-language forums as a private MaaS since December 2025, has compromised thousands of devices across the META region through a streaming-app-to-dropper chain, draining retail banking accounts via full Accessibility Service takeover.
Key findings:
- The infection chain starts on Google Play, not a phishing SMS. A low-reputation streaming app serves malicious ad banners that deliver a dropper outside the store. A confirmed dropper observed during this research impersonates "TikTok 18+" and installs the Mirax payload, which then presents itself as "Google Play Services" using a Cyrillic homoglyph substitution to pass visual inspection. On-device automation actively coerces the victim into granting Accessibility Service, the single permission that hands the operator real-time control: keylogging, SMS and OTP interception, screen sharing, VNC, and autonomous device unlock using the captured PIN, password, or pattern.
- Mirax is a private MaaS sold by a developer using the handle MiraxBot, with access restricted to vetted affiliates and priority given to established Russian-speaking actors. A February 2026 update added a SOCKS5 module that turns each infected phone into a residential proxy node, routing fraudulent transactions through the victim's own IP address to defeat geolocation and IP-reputation controls. From the bank's perspective, the session, the device, the app, and the location all look legitimate.
- The "aquafina" build tag ties all samples in this campaign to a single operation targeting 20+ META-region retail banks and digital wallets, plus a small number of global cryptocurrency exchanges. The same tag was observed reporting to more than one C2 host. Package names are randomized per build, the launcher icon is hidden at runtime (no drawer entry exists), and the app name rotates to stay ahead of takedown. Activity spiked over the Eid holiday period and again at the end of July 2026, and the campaign was still running at time of publication.
- The core evasion is server-side capability. HTML overlay templates, their target-app bindings, C2 host, ports, TLS parameters, DNS-over-HTTPS config, and polling intervals are all pushed from the C2 after install and are absent from the APK entirely. Static analysis of the installed sample shows only what Mirax could do, not what it is configured to do. DNS-over-HTTPS is on by default, keeping C2 resolution off local and carrier DNS. Transport runs over dual WebSocket channels (one for commands, one for exfiltration) with an HTTP long-poll fallback. Persistence is maintained through Android Broadcast Receivers, surviving reboots; anti-removal blocks the uninstall screen and can prevent security apps from launching.
- Estimated losses reach into the millions of US 🇺🇸 dollars, covering only confirmed cases. Unauthorized international transfers were routed to accounts abroad, with evidence suggesting mule accounts in India 🇮🇳 were used to move and launder funds. IOCs in the report include 19 SHA1 file hashes with their randomized package names (installation dates ranging from late June through early August 2026) and two C2 domains: oscofneuid[.]com and kenobuias[.]com. The full C2 command inventory (70+ commands including startVncScreenSharing, unlockDevice, socks5_enable, blackScreen_updating, and addExternalHtmlTemplate) is in the report appendix.
Practitioner takeaway: Static APK analysis will miss most of what Mirax actually does in a live deployment. For fraud and SOC teams, the detection surface that matters is behavioral: Accessibility Service grants from non-accessibility apps, screen-sharing or VNC session activity coinciding with active banking transactions, and outbound DoH traffic masking C2 resolution. Flag any transaction attempted while remote-control indicators are present and hold it for verification before funds move. Add oscofneuid[.]com and kenobuias[.]com to your blocklists and monitor for the randomized package name pattern (short random strings under io, net, org, com namespaces) combined with a hidden launcher icon. The full IOC set and C2 command inventory are in the Group-IB report.

item.title: 警惕 cwpdoor：寄生在 Control Web Panel 中的零检出被动后门
item.description:
Zero-detection passive backdoor "cwpdoor" parasitizes CentOS Web Panel's own web server binary, targeting 340,000+ exposed CWP instances worldwide with a triple-layer stealth technique combining binary replacement, passive trigger, and log suppression.
Key findings:
- cwpdoor is not a standalone implant. Attackers compiled malicious code directly into cwpsrv source (the Nginx-based web server that powers CWP's control panel), then deployed it via a dropper script (MD5: e505d4ffa21cf494a5dc2d7c8f4f1236) disguised as a "version update." The script runs as root, replaces /usr/local/cwpsrv/bin/cwpsrv with a trojaned binary (MD5: 965aea67fb40de1bab5169ada993349f for v1.15.10, d3f4e95113d49ab3991b45e457bda75b for v1.24.0), then deliberately restores original atime/mtime timestamps on both the binary and its parent directory, and runs "history -d" to erase shell history. Standard "ls" and "stat" checks will show no modification. The dropper communicates back to 136.0.141[.]71 with the result.
- The backdoor trigger is a three-header HTTP handshake: X-Ngx-Integrity-Time (timestamp, validated within a 300-second window for anti-replay), X-Ngx-Integrity-Sig (RSA signature over the concatenated time and data values, verified against an XOR-obfuscated embedded public key), and X-Ngx-Integrity-Data (AES-256-CBC encrypted command, IV in the first 16 bytes, key derived from SHA256 of the embedded RSA public key string). Only if all three pass does the main process decrypt the command and relay it over Unix domain socket ngx_http_integrity_helper to a persistent helper child process for execution. Results return as an AES-encrypted application/octet-stream 200 response.
- Log suppression is built into the trigger path. When a valid backdoor request is handled, cwpdoor copies the request's module context array and replaces the log module's context pointer, preventing the request from ever reaching access logs. No web log entry is written for attacker interaction. Combined with the timestamp-forged binary, this closes the forensic loop: no file modification evidence, no log evidence.
- Real-world victims confirmed. A file named evidencia.tgz was uploaded to VirusTotal from Brazil 🇧🇷 on September 30, 2026, containing both a known Ebury SSH backdoor and cwpsrv.suspeito, which is cwpdoor, with a detection rate of zero across all vendors at the time of upload. XLab's report notes the relationship between Ebury and cwpdoor on the same host is unconfirmed: potentially two independent actors, potentially coordinated. Either way, the implant has real victims.
- Three fast triage commands tie directly to cwpdoor's artifacts. Run "ss -axp | grep integrity" to check for the Unix domain socket ngx_http_integrity_helper. Run "ps aux | grep cwpsrv" and look for an unexpected helper child process. Run "strings /usr/local/cwpsrv/bin/cwpsrv | grep X-Ngx-Integrity" and flag any match. If compromised, the dropper script leaves the legitimate binary at /usr/local/cwpsrv/bin/cwpsrv.prev-[timestamp], which can be used for direct restoration before upgrading CWP and rotating all panel credentials, which should be treated as fully compromised.
Hunt now: on any CWP host, those three commands take under a minute. The initial dropper pulls from hxxp://136.0.141[.]71/static/cwpsrv_update.sh, hxxp://136.0.141[.]71/static/cwpsrv_1.15.10, and hxxp://136.0.141[.]71/static/cwpsrv_1.24.0. Check web proxy and firewall logs for outbound connections to 136.0.141[.]71. IOCs and sample hashes are in the XLab report.

The initial dropper pulls from hxxp://136.0.141[.]71/static/cwpsrv_update.sh, hxxp://136.0.141[.]71/static/cwpsrv_1.15.10, and hxxp://136.0.141[.]71/static/cwpsrv_1.24.0. Check web proxy and firewall logs for outbound connections to 136.0.141[.]71. IOCs and sample hashes are in the XLab report.

item.title: SlippyNunchucks hijacks Sogou Input Method’s brand promotion mechanism to distribute malware
item.description:
China-aligned SlippyNunchucks hijacks Sogou Input Method's brand promotion HTTP endpoint via DNS manipulation to drop the DarkVigil modular implant on Chinese-speaking targets across Asia and Europe, patched in Sogou version 16.10 (CVE-2026-120422).
Key findings:
- SlippyNunchucks (active since at least September 2023, distinct from Mustang Panda per ESET's telemetry) has consistently abused popular Chinese 🇨🇳 applications including Sogou Input Method, QuickFox, QingTalk, MiYunChat, SoftCam, and tawk[.]to to reach Chinese-speaking diaspora targets. Victims span Hong Kong, Thailand 🇹🇭, Japan 🇯🇵, Vietnam 🇻🇳, Oman, and Sri Lanka 🇱🇰, with European individuals in Germany 🇩🇪, Russia 🇷🇺, the UK 🇬🇧, and Austria 🇦🇹 also hit. The targeting of a multinational Chinese-language gambling operator aligns with Chinese 🇨🇳 state enforcement interest in overseas gambling activity, reinforcing the nation-state surveillance assessment.
- The attack abuses SGTool.exe, a legitimate Sogou component, which sends an unencrypted HTTP GET to config.pinyin.sogou[.]com/api/brandScd/getBrandScd.php (the brand promotion icon config endpoint, invoked via --appid=scdreg -update). DNS resolution for that host was redirected to attacker-controlled staging servers at 47.239.250[.]102 or 47.237.122[.]175, both serving the spoofed domain sogou-cdn[.]com. Those servers returned a maliciously crafted AES-256-CBC encrypted config (key and IV embedded in SGTool.exe's .rdata section) with modified md5 integrity fields pointing to attacker payloads, bypassing the application's own validation.
- The malicious config drops two payloads into Sogou's Components directory: a legitimate signed Adobe Licensing WF Helper renamed biz_helper.exe (SHA-1: 79188C8DE2378B437D39E867475C5B4714A0D7C9) placed as SogouComMgr.exe, and the DarkVigil implant as libcef.dll (SHA-1: 8A60A8E90E1F5F08F28FE5A6DD57BD686C20DC23). Whenever SGTool.exe invokes SogouComMgr.exe for component install or load operations (e.g., -invoke BizCenterComBundle BizCenterCom), it instead executes the Adobe binary, which side-loads the malicious libcef.dll. No separate persistence mechanism is needed: the implant hijacks Sogou's own component management workflow (T1574.001, T1036.005).
- DarkVigil is a modular .NET toolset built on the Vigil framework, itself built on TouchSocket and its Duplex Message Transport Protocol (DMTP). DMTP operates over TCP, UDP, HTTP, WebSocket, or named pipes, identified by the magic header bytes "dm". Plugins are pushed from C2, stored compressed in the registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\IME\<HWID>\pluginHash (T1112), then decompressed, loaded into the .NET runtime, and executed. Each plugin establishes its own indirect DMTP channel back to C2 via the implant as relay, with a PluginID built from ProtocolType, HWID, controlerID, randomID, and PluginName (e.g., "Pillager"). Bootstrap domains include blog.wangmengfun[.]top, update.mssproxy[.]net, and img.fusfun[.]top. Staging/hijacking infrastructure includes 47.236.254[.]159 at dev.soft-png-cdn[.]com and sogou-cdn[.]com.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt for SGTool.exe spawning unexpected child processes or making outbound HTTP connections to any host other than Tencent-owned infrastructure. Check the Sogou Components directory for biz_helper.exe masquerading as SogouComMgr.exe and for an unsigned libcef.dll. Query HKCU\Software\Microsoft\IME for subkeys matching a HWID pattern containing a pluginHash value: compressed plugin binaries stored there are a strong indicator of active DarkVigil deployment. Verify DNS resolution history for config.pinyin.sogou[.]com in network logs and DNS cache artifacts. The full IOC list and samples are in ESET's GitHub repository. Update Sogou Input Method to version 16.10 or later, which migrates the affected requests to HTTPS with certificate pinning, closing the hijack surface.

item.title: Detection Engineering: Implementing Detection-as-Code in an Existing Environment: Part 2: Execution
item.description:
Detection-as-Code migration in practice: NVISO Labs details the execution phase of consolidating scattered detection data into a single Git repository, covering data restructuring, Git history preservation, and automated artifact generation for Splunk and other platforms.
Key findings:
- The core technical challenge was schema quality, not architecture. Many metadata documents stored on file shares had character encoding errors, missing keys, null bytes, and indentation faults that were invisible in the old workflow but broke machine parsing entirely. NVISO built a parsing library using strictyaml and jsonschema to validate every file against a defined schema, then corrected issues in two passes: semi-automated scripts for encoding problems, and manual file-by-file correction for structural errors. Detection teams inheriting legacy rule sets should expect this same debt before any pipeline can be automated reliably.
- Preserving Git history through the restructuring required deliberate commit sequencing. Because Git infers file moves by comparing content similarity rather than recording moves directly, the team split every change into two commits: one that changed file content while keeping paths identical, and a second that moved or renamed files without touching content. This kept git blame intact across the restructured repository. The --allow-unrelated-histories flag was required to merge branches from multiple formerly separate repositories into a single local integration repo before pushing back to GitHub.
- Splunk deployment artifact generation was fully scripted. The script iterated each detection folder, read the target Splunk app from meta.yml, and concatenated the detection's splunk-searches.conf, splunk-transforms.conf, and splunk-macros.conf snippets into the corresponding app-level savedsearches.conf, transforms.conf, and macros.conf files. Lookup files were copied unchanged. This means the detection repository becomes the authoritative input and the Splunk app directory becomes a generated output, not a place engineers edit directly.
- Atomic Red Team test files created duplication that required post-migration cleanup. Because test case naming was inconsistent, the migration script could not reliably match individual test cases to individual detections. The safe fallback was to copy the full test script into every detection folder sharing the same MITRE ATT&CK technique. That duplication was resolved post-migration through partial automation where naming allowed, and manual investigation where it did not. Teams running similar migrations should treat ART test mapping as a separate cleanup workstream, not an inline step.
- Excel reports were the last data silo. Regulatory and internal reporting requirements meant the spreadsheets had to remain, but after migration they became generated outputs. The metadata schema was extended to cover any fields the Excel reports required that meta.yml did not already contain, a script migrated existing metadata to the new schema, and CLI tooling was built to populate and refresh the reports directly from the GitHub repository on demand.
Practitioner takeaway: if your detection repository migration keeps stalling, the NVISO approach of dry-running the full migration against a copy of production data and diffing generated artifacts against pre-migration files is the most reliable way to surface hidden issues before the freeze window opens. Start with schema validation on every metadata file before writing a single migration script, and plan your Git commit strategy around the two-step content-then-move sequence if history preservation matters to your team.

item.title: APT29-Linked Hackers Hijack Web Analytics Script to Deliver iOS and Android Exploits
item.description:
APT29-linked "Poisoned Source" campaign hijacks a Ukrainian 🇺🇦 web analytics supply chain and watering holes to deliver iOS and Android N-day exploit kits against high-value targets, including military, defense, and government-adjacent sites tied to the Russia-Ukraine war.
Three infection vectors converge on the same JavaScript profiler, then fork into platform-specific exploitation:
- Supply chain entry point: Between August 27 and September 3, 2026, APT29-linked actors injected malicious code into a.plerdy[.]com/public/js/click/main.js, the script tag for Plerdy SEO Tracker, a Ukrainian 🇺🇦 analytics service. Any site loading that script during that window silently profiled every visitor. Compromised watering holes also include a U.S. 🇺🇸 chemical industry trade association, a European far-right political party, and a Bulgarian 🇧🇬 military-related website. Lookalike domains impersonating high-profile properties, including america250[.]holiday, complete the three-vector picture.
- iOS exploit chains: Class A targets iOS 16.7, chaining CVE-2025-43529 and CVE-2024-27834 to steal browser cookies via JavaScript malware. Class B targets iOS 18.5 and runs the full DarkSword kit across five CVEs: CVE-2025-43529, CVE-2026-20700, CVE-2025-14174, CVE-2025-43510, and CVE-2025-43520, pulling SMS, iMessages, Apple Mail SQLite databases (Envelope Index and Protected Index), voicemail, WhatsApp and Telegram databases, iCloud Keychain, Wi-Fi passwords, contacts, call history, Safari history and cookies, photos, and data from Health, Calendar, Notes, and iCloud Drive. No tap, no install, no warning required.
- Android exploit chain (AndroSnitch): Class C targets Chrome versions 139 through 145, excluding 143 for unknown reasons, exploiting CVE-2026-3910 and CVE-2025-27038 for remote code execution, sandbox escape, and privilege escalation. The resulting payload, AndroSnitch, collects Chrome data and Wi-Fi passwords. The chain explicitly checks the device model identifier SM-S938B (Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra) and aborts if matched, a deliberate evasion or targeting decision. All exfiltrated data routes to ad.starx-net[.]com:8881/telemetry/v12.
- Coruna and DarkSword proliferation beyond APT29: The DeadTag criminal campaign acquires expired analytics and ad-tag domains still loaded by thousands of sites, serving Coruna (targeting iOS 13 through 17.2.1) and DarkSword P7 (iOS 18.4 through 18.7) to iPhone visitors while returning nothing to bots or scanners. As of October 2026 Zimperium zLabs counted 608 domains delivering Coruna-family code. Coruna has leaked beyond its original nation-state developer and is now accessible to multiple threat actors. Lure sites often explicitly instruct users to leave in-app browsers and open links in Safari to satisfy the exploit chain's requirements.
DFIR takeaway: On mobile incident response, start with the browser's SQLite databases and the data stores the report enumerates: Apple Mail indexes, iCloud Keychain, WhatsApp and Telegram databases, and Safari cookies, all consistent with Class B DarkSword exfiltration. For Android cases, examine Chrome profile data and saved Wi-Fi credentials. Network forensics should hunt for outbound connections to ad.starx-net[.]com:8881/telemetry/v12. For enterprise exposure assessment, audit any third-party JavaScript tags loaded by your web properties and check whether Plerdy SEO Tracker was present during the August 27 to September 3 window. IOCs and the full technical breakdown are in the Sekoia report.

item.title: What happens when a fake coding test reaches a security company?
item.description:
North Korean 🇰🇵 fake-interview campaigns hit a security vendor: BeaverTail and InvisibleFerret deployed via a VS Code workspace lure, exposing a broken endpoint agent as the critical failure point.
Key details:
- The attack chain began with a GitHub "coding assignment" opened in VS Code. A command hidden in the workspace settings file executed the moment a terminal opened, delivering the BeaverTail loader and InvisibleFerret backdoor within two minutes. The first script dropped on the Mac was detected as Troj/Dloadr-EJE, but the endpoint agent was broken, so detection never fired. The Binance variant took a different path: attackers swapped the legitimate pyenv component inside a Homebrew installation for a malicious version, used it to beacon an attacker-controlled server, then cleaned traces. Both chains abused trusted developer tooling rather than exploit code.
- The compromised Mac was only discovered via an external tip through an intelligence-sharing channel, not internal controls. The root cause was mundane: the endpoint agent had stopped reporting. The vendor's existing device-compliance checks and coverage monitoring had a gap because they were not correlated with identity sign-in data. A device actively authenticating but silent in the endpoint console is a blind spot. Correlating those two data sources surfaced the gap. The full root cause analysis is published as INC-2026-002.
- Attribution from Sophos CTU points to NICKEL ALLEY (Contagious Interview), whose tradecraft matches the VS Code workspace technique, fake companies, malicious code repositories, ClickFix lures, and poisoned npm packages. NICKEL GLADSTONE, the financially focused subgroup, is FBI-linked to the Binance attack under the TraderTraitor label. A September joint advisory from Japan's 🇯🇵 National Police Agency and the FBI assessed that between December 2025 and July 2026, Contagious Interview (also named WaterPlum) compromised at least 30,000 devices across more than 100 countries and drained over 7,000 cryptocurrency wallets.
- Lateral movement at Binance used an internal AI tool to pivot from one engineer to two others, underscoring that AI-layer access needs the same containment thinking as any privileged service: credential isolation, sealed tool endpoints, and human approval gates for irreversible actions.
Practitioner takeaway: Pull every device that has authenticated to your identity provider in the last 30 days and cross-reference against your endpoint console's active device list. Any device that is signing in but not reporting is an unmonitored asset and your highest-priority coverage gap. For the VS Code lure specifically, audit workspace settings files (settings.json and tasks.json inside .vscode directories in any cloned repository) for terminal or task entries that run scripts on open. BeaverTail and InvisibleFerret are your hunt targets on macOS; look for unexpected child processes spawned from the VS Code helper process and outbound connections established within seconds of a terminal open event.

item.title: Application identity abuse targets MSPs and customer environments
item.description:
Application identity abuse targets MSPs-linked threat actor authenticates as trusted Azure apps, bypassing MFA entirely, to harvest credentials across multiple customer tenants in an ongoing campaign first observed November 1, 2026.
Key findings:
- The adversary authenticated directly to Microsoft Entra ID and Azure DevOps using valid application credentials, operating as trusted service principals rather than compromised users. Because application sign-ins carry no interactive session, MFA and user-focused Conditional Access policies do not apply, and on-premises firewalls have no visibility. All confirmed malicious activity originated from a single IP: 199.19.77[.]84, hosted in Poland 🇵🇱.
- Once authenticated, the operator retrieved stored secrets from Key Vault and other credential stores, then used MSP multi-tenant applications, Partner Center tokens, and Granular Delegated Admin Privileges (GDAP) applications to pivot across customer tenants. Previously dormant applications began authenticating within minutes of secret retrieval, confirming the operator moved laterally using freshly harvested credentials. Azure DevOps service connections and deployment pipelines were in scope, introducing risk to production infrastructure.
- The operator collected files containing credentials and configuration details for VPNs, RMM tools, backup platforms, and firewalls. Access to those downstream systems is the likely end goal, extending the breach well beyond the Microsoft cloud. Integration applications for security tooling, including Todyl's own MSP integration apps in two tenants, were among the credentials abused, with no evidence of vendor platform compromise.
- After detections fired on November 3, 2026, the adversary adapted: spoofing browser signatures, replaying users' refresh tokens, and retrying disabled and rotated application credentials in fixed 11-second loops. Conditional Access blocked every token replay observed that day, and error codes AADSTS7000215 and AADSTS7000222 appeared in logs alongside failed secret attempts followed by successful sign-ins, a detectable pattern.
Practitioner takeaway: Pull Entra ID service principal sign-in logs and filter for 199.19.77[.]84, then hunt for the sequence of AADSTS7000215 or AADSTS7000222 errors followed by a successful authentication, and for applications authenticating after extended inactivity. For confirmed exposure, remove all secrets, certificates, and federated credentials on affected service principals, check for credentials added without approval, and disable the principal. Already-issued tokens remain valid until expiry, so also revoke Azure DevOps PATs and SSH keys and rotate every downstream credential the application could reach: VPN, RMM, backup, and firewall. Block 199.19.77[.]84 via a Conditional Access named location policy scoped to workload identities and to user sessions covering token replay. IOCs and detailed mitigation steps are in the report.

item.title: CVE-2026-119977: When Updating WordPress Becomes the Vulnerability
item.description:
CVE-2026-119977 (CVSS 8.1): Unauthenticated RCE in WordPress core updater via race condition, actively exploited in the wild and added to CISA KEV on November 3, 2026. Fixed in WordPress 7.1.4.
Key findings:
- The race window opens between WordPress extracting a core update package into wp-content/upgrade/[package-name]/wordpress/ and copying it over the live site. The temporary setup-config.php does not search upward far enough to find the live wp-config.php, so it treats the staging tree as an unconfigured installation and runs the setup wizard without authentication. An attacker who wins the race can POST database credentials to that temporary installer, which writes a malicious wp-config.php into the staging tree at wp-content/upgrade/[package-name]/wordpress/wp-config.php. Because wp-config.php is absent from both the initial skip list and the checksum manifest, the updater copies it straight over /var/www/html/wp-config.php. The live site then connects to the attacker's empty database, re-exposes the install wizard, and an attacker-created administrator account can upload a PHP plugin for RCE.
- Exploitability depends on whether the staging path is predictable. WordPress 2.7.0-2.7.1 used the fixed path wp-content/upgrade/core. Versions 2.8.0-4.3.35 derived the directory name from the package filename with no random suffix, also predictable. Versions 4.4.0-5.8.18 added a six-character random suffix, making the path unpredictable unless disclosed through verbose errors or other means. Versions 5.9.0-7.1.3 reintroduced predictability by honoring the Content-Disposition filename from the package server, so a stable server-supplied name like wordpress-7.0.3[.]zip produces wp-content/upgrade/wordpress-7.0.3 deterministically.
- The 7.1.4 patch applies three changes: a 16-character random suffix is now added to the working directory name in class-wp-upgrader.php directly, so the Content-Disposition rename can no longer determine the path; upgrade/index.php is preserved across cleanups to block directory listing from leaking the random name on servers with indexing enabled; and wp-config.php is explicitly added to the skip list in update-core.php. However, the update that installs the fix is itself still partially exposed: unpack_package() runs from the old code and still creates a predictable staging path, so the temporary installer is still reachable during that one transition update. The new update-core.php does skip wp-config.php, so the live config cannot be overwritten during this window, but an attacker can still configure the temporary copy with their own database and execute PHP with web server privileges before the staging directory is cleaned up.
- Affected range is WordPress 2.7.0 through 7.1.3. The fix was backported to all maintained branches down to 4.7. Versions 2.7 through 4.6 received no backport and must be upgraded to a supported release. The wp core update WP-CLI command uses the same underlying updater and extracts into wp-content/upgrade/ identically, so it is not a safe substitute for a manual update during the transition.
DFIR and detection angle: Requests hitting setup-config.php under wp-content/upgrade/ are the clearest signal of exploitation in progress. Web server access logs are your primary evidence source. Look for POST requests to paths matching /wp-content/upgrade/*/wordpress/wp-admin/setup-config.php originating from unexpected source IPs during or shortly after a core update event. A modified wp-config.php timestamp that postdates the update start time but predates the update completion is a strong indicator of successful config replacement. If you suspect compromise, compare the DB_HOST, DB_NAME, and DB_USER values in the live wp-config.php against your known configuration. As an immediate mitigation before patching, block web access to wp-content/upgrade/ at the server level: on Nginx with "location ^~ /wp-content/upgrade/ { deny all; }" or on Apache with "Require all denied" in the Directory block. Confirm the path returns 403 before triggering any update. For the safest transition to 7.1.4, extract the release to /tmp outside the web root and rsync wp-admin and wp-includes into place while explicitly excluding wp-config.php and wp-content, then run wp-admin/upgrade.php to complete database updates.

item.title: How Cortex AES Protects Against Compromised Claude Code Extensions
item.description:
Malicious versions of the Claude Code VS Code extension were distributed through Cursor's marketplace for 11 hours, exposing up to 5,000 developers to a supply chain attack carrying reconnaissance, persistence, and SSH backdoor capabilities.
Key details:
- Compromised versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 of anthropic.claude-code were pushed through Cursor's Open VSX-mirrored marketplace on October 29, 2026, targeting macOS and Windows. The malicious payload lived inside the extension's extension.js bundle (SHA-256: ecb58cb29078d9646ad1dcdbe51526f2d9cfea06be5fb2ab183e8ecc3ab6bf15) and was not authored by Anthropic. The root cause traces to a vulnerability in Open VSX's publisher verification and namespace management that allowed full marketplace account takeover, meaning a poisoned update could reach developers without triggering standard trust warnings.
- Once loaded, the extension ran host reconnaissance: collecting OS details, usernames, working directories, public IP addresses, and environment variable names, then beaconing to 134.209.82[.]225:8099/beacon over HTTP. It also attempted to inject an unauthorized SSH public key (comment: svc-telemetry, fingerprint SHA256:0Z6R+DF64Do2nwQic8a7kkfDLNNk4IiK+2U2Rci4htk) into authorized_keys and open a reverse SSH tunnel to that same C2 over TCP port 22.
- Persistence was attempted via a macOS LaunchAgent (com[.]apple.sysmond.plist) and a Windows scheduled task named SysMon, with supporting artifacts at .config/.smt and .config/smt.cmd. Errors in the payload and lack of admin privileges generally prevented the SSH backdoor from going fully operational, but persistence mechanisms and telemetry transmission could still succeed even without elevated rights.
- The attacker-controlled infrastructure at 134.209.82[.]225 is now offline and the compromised versions have been pulled, but any endpoint that loaded these versions during the 11-hour window should be treated as potentially implanted. Developer systems routinely hold source-control tokens, cloud keys, registry credentials, and active sessions, making credential exposure the most consequential downstream risk here.
Responder action: audit installed extension versions across developer endpoints and flag any system that had anthropic.claude-code 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 active between October 29 and 30, 2026. On those hosts, hunt for the svc-telemetry authorized_keys entry, com[.]apple.sysmond.plist, the SysMon scheduled task, and the .config/smt.cmd artifact. Check endpoint and network telemetry for outbound connections to 134.209.82[.]225. Isolate any host showing evidence of payload execution, strip all malicious artifacts, and rotate every credential class accessible from that environment from a clean host. Full platform-specific verification commands and remediation scripts are in Cursor's official security notice.

item.title: Mi Scusi, My SCSI: Abusing iSCSI Target Server
item.description:
Unauthenticated iSCSI target abuse lets an attacker impersonate a legitimate initiator, mount virtual hard disks over the network, and walk away with NTDS.dit and credential hives, bypassing NTFS entirely.
Key findings:
- Discovery starts with a simple LDAP query: when the Windows iSCSI Target Server service starts, it registers an SPN on the host computer's AD account, handing attackers a ready-made list of targets. Initiator IQNs are equally predictable, constructed from the dNSHostName attribute of domain-joined computers in the format iqn.1991-05[.]com[.]microsoft:hostname.domain. No rate limiting or brute-force protection exists on the service, so iterating through AD or DNS computer names is cheap.
- Without CHAP configured, the iSCSI Login Phase requires only three things: the target server's address, its target IQN, and a recognized initiator IQN. The target IQN is recoverable via an unauthenticated Discovery session using the SendTargets operation, which the RFC mandates the server answer with every IQN the querying initiator can access. The tool scuzzy[.]py automates this enumeration and login sequence.
- Because iSCSI operates at block level, a successful connection bypasses NTFS permissions entirely. An attacker who mounts the volume can browse the file system as if seated at the storage layer, including the $RECYCLE.BIN directory, which leaks SIDs of users who had interactive logons on hosts that previously mounted the volume.
- The worst-case path lands domain compromise in a single chain: enumerate SPN in AD, brute-force initiator IQNs, run a Discovery session to recover the target IQN, login, download the .VHDX of a Hyper-V VM that happens to be a domain controller, mount it with adiskreader, and extract SAM, SYSTEM, SECURITY, and NTDS.dit from C:\Windows\System32\config and C:\Windows\NTDS, then run Impacket's secretsdump[.]py against the recovered files. BitLocker or equivalent encryption breaks this chain; absent that, the drive is an open book.
- SpecterOps queried BloodHound Enterprise customer tenants and found roughly 50% had at least one computer with the iSCSI target SPN registered, with one tenant showing close to 700 such hosts. Common payloads on these drives include clustered Hyper-V VMs, MSSQL, Exchange DAGs, and third-party backup data.
Hunt: query AD for SPNs containing "MicrosoftInternetSCSITarget" or the equivalent host-class SPN the service registers to map your exposure. For hosts that show up, audit the iSCSI target configuration for CHAP enforcement and check whether the access server list contains any broad or wildcard initiator entries. Network captures on TCP port 3260 showing Discovery session traffic from unexpected initiators are your canary. Enable CHAP authentication, enforce IPsec for iSCSI traffic to prevent credential sniffing, and use host-based firewall rules to restrict TCP 3260 to known initiator IPs rather than relying on IQN identity alone.
